title: I’m building Hearth & Fortune with AI help. Getting the woodland to look right took more than passing checks.
author: IconicXPGames

replies.author: IconicXPGames
replies.body: Yep, Unreal! I started in Unity. It took 36 hours straight to migrate, then another full week to clean it up. Painful, but worth it for what I want Hearth & Fortune to become. Still learning as I go!

replies.author: IconicXPGames
replies.body: Thank you! I’m really happy with how it’s coming along. Starting in Unity helped me follow along and learn a lot. I’d never done anything like this before, so seeing how far the game has come makes all the effort worth it.

comments.author: Bitter-College8786
comments.body:
What made you switch from Unity to Unreal?  
And how did you get the 3D assets? From Unreal store or Blender or Meshy / Tripo?

replies.author: IconicXPGames
replies.body:
The planned scope was the main reason: a medieval world with NPC families, businesses and trade between settlements, changing over generations. Online advice and AI guidance pointed me toward Unreal for that ambition and the visuals. I wouldn’t say Unity couldn’t do it. I debated for a long time, but worried I'd get too far to change engines later. Unreal felt like the better fit.

The migration took 36 hours straight of AI running, then another week cleaning things up. Painful, but I’m happy with the decision. Starting in Unity helped me learn a lot.

Assets are a mix of Unity Asset Store purchases licensed for use in Unreal and assets from Fab/Unreal Marketplace. Right now I’m experimenting with AI-assisted design for MetaHuman clothing. Hoping to have pictures to share by the end of the week!

replies.author: IconicXPGames
replies.body: I still have both the Unity and Unreal builds from around the migration available to testers. They give a pretty honest picture of where things stood during the switch, all the rough edges from both sides included!

comments.author: WriterFreelance
comments.body: You dude. You want advice for trees? Love the visuals BTW!

replies.author: IconicXPGames
replies.body: Absolutely, and thank you! I’d welcome advice. The upper tree trunks still look smooth and grey compared with the roots. We traced part of it to the Unity assets using two blended bark layers that weren’t transferring correctly to Unreal, plus differences in texture mapping. We spent hours trying to fix it, but I’m still not happy with the result. What would you suggest?

replies.author: WriterFreelance
replies.body:
Do this. If you have a good image gen. Do a multishot of a tree with your best image gen. But do a multishot without leafs. Leafs screw it up. Mesh the multishot with a good image to 3d.
Also if your feeling technical. Do a multishot with just major branches. And then make a mesh of a tree with only major branches, 20 to 30 different types of the same tree species, with fine branches.
If you got codex get it to node branches with leafs separate.
Then have it do a texture run of leafs and bark, have it run several. Have it connect the nodes branches on your tree.
Find a professional version of that tree and make a rolladex comparing that professional tree to a tree with random branches(via nodes on the branches with leafs made in blender) for you to inspect.
Then you got a relatively random version of the same tree mesh.

I did this on my project it makes the trees not to data heavy and lookin random.

If you need me to explain further. I can have my codex describe the whole thing in a short summary.

replies.author: IconicXPGames
replies.body: Yes please, a short summary would be really useful. Which image-to-3D tool did you use, and how did you handle bark UVs, branch joins, wind and exporting the Blender instances into the game engine? Was your project in Unreal?

replies.author: WriterFreelance
replies.body: No unity...I thought about unreal but im so far in.

replies.author: WriterFreelance
replies.body: I used meshy for much of the work. Would recommend if you have alot of object meshy is good for the first month. Not worth 100 a month tho.
